query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a uniform, thin nickel (Ni) interlayer on the tungsten surfaces of a W–Cu composite will mitigate phase separation and suppress interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, thereby enhancing thermal conductivity compared to an untreated composite.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
generation.intervention: Deposit a conformal, thin Ni coating (via chemical vapor deposition or a similar precise method) on the tungsten surfaces prior to composite assembly.
generation.conditions: Operating conditions that involve thermal cycling and irradiation typical for joints between tungsten-based plasma-facing components and copper-based cooling systems.
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface that ensures improved interfacial bonding and reduces local interfacial energy mismatches.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating acts as a diffusion barrier and wetting promoter, reducing the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation, minimizing interfacial void nucleation, and thus preserving a more coherent interface under thermal and irradiation stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated composite will exhibit a more stable microstructure with lower void formation and higher thermal conductivity relative to untreated composites when subjected to similar service conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites that, under heat-transfer and irradiation, tend to suffer from phase separation and interfacial void formation, leading to degraded thermal performance.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the Ni interlayer may be limited by factors such as coating thickness uniformity and potential Ni diffusion at extreme temperatures or prolonged irradiation beyond optimized service limits.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the Ni coating under extended irradiation and high thermal loads is uncertain and requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one with a pre-deposited thin Ni coating on tungsten phases and one without any coating. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation tests under conditions simulating service joints. Use microscopy (e.g., TEM) to assess interfacial structures and void formation, and measure thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis.
measurements: Quantification of interfacial void fractions via TEM
Elemental diffusion profiles (EDS) to check coating integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in interfacial void formation and corresponding improvements in thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composites under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
